Ladies and gentleman, settle down. We’re about to begin. Good morning. Good morning. Welcome to the New York City Council hearing on the Committee of Early Childhood Education. Welcome to the first hearing of the Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education. I’m your Chair, Jennifer Gutiérrez. We would like to start with Speaker Menin who’s joined us this morning.

Thank you so much, Chair, and good morning, and I just want to welcome everyone to today’s first-ever hearing of the newly established subcommittee on Early Childhood Education. I’m Julie Menin, Speaker of the New York City Council, and I first of all want to begin by thanking my colleague, Chair Jennifer Gutiérrez, who is Chair of this new Subcommittee for joining me in

convening this incredibly important hearing on the path to Universal Childcare. I was proud to not only create this new subcommittee as one of my first acts of Speaker, but I’m also proud to have appointed Council Member Gutiérrez as the Chair. I know this issue is incredibly personal to her, and that she will be a strong and powerful voice in helping New Yorkers with all issues related to child care in our city. At today’s hearing, we’ll also be hearing a package of eight pieces of legislation which Chair Gutiérrez will outline shortly. I’m proud to be sponsoring two of these pieces of legislation, Intro. 8 in relation to establishing a pilot program to make vacant commercial premises suitable for use by child care programs, and Intro. 9 in relation to a study and report on expediting the child care permitting process. Though this subcommittee is new to the Council, the issue of universal child care is an issue that has come up time and time again over the last four years, and I’m thrilled that it will finally be getting the attention that it deserves. As Chair Gutiérrez will also discuss, in 2022, the Council passed a package of legislation that was aimed at putting the city on a path to universal

child care. I was proud to have been the sponsor of five pieces of legislation in that package, and while the Council passed those bills and Mayor Adams signed the bills, unfortunately, those bills were not fully implemented by the Adams administration. Now, the city has an opportunity and quite frankly an obligation to provide universal child care for New Yorkers. Now is the right time. We have tremendous alignment and consensus on this issue across the political spectrum, and between branches of government. In January, I stood shoulder to shoulder with the Governor, the Mayor, and with Chair Gutiérrez and a number of our colleagues to announce the expansion of child care programs for New Yorkers. Now is the time for our city to finally achieve universal child care. We truly cannot afford to wait any longer. When we talk about universal child care, many people immediately say universal child care is too expensive. That response is frankly backwards. Our economy requires universal child care. Let’s be honest. The backbone of our economy is parents, and really, it’s mothers. Mothers are the ones that cannot fully participate in our workforce, in our economy, and in our society when child care remains

as unaffordable and inaccessible as it currently is. Last year alone, approximately 300,000 parents left the workforce, mainly mothers, because they could not afford child care. That is not only morally wrong, it is also fiscally disastrous. The loss of those parents from our workforce cost the city around $2.2 billion a year in lost economic output, all due to unaffordable child care. We cannot afford to continue with business as usual. We need child care that is quality, affordable, and accessible, and we need it now. I also recognize that this is not going to be an easy fight. There are many barriers to providing universal child care, even apart from the cost. We need to build out a skilled and well-compensated workforce. We need to identify safe and appropriate spaces. We need to cut through layers and layers of confusing license requirements and bureaucracy, and importantly, we need to build out a system that accounts for the many diverse communities that live in the city and assure that what we create works for everyone. But I’m also confident that these challenges should not be a reason that we do not achieve this goal. We have a lot of existing infrastructure, for example, through

a UPK and U3K, through our Department of Education, through our wonderful not-for-profit workforce, and that we can build on to ultimately realize universal child care. We at the Council are ready to roll up our sleeves and do the work necessary to achieve universal child care for New Yorkers. I’m looking forward to hearing from the administration at this hearing on where we stand today in achieving this goal together as partners in government. And now, let me turn it back to Chair Gutiérrez. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON GUTIÉRREZ: Thank you, Speaker Menin. Thank you for this new subcommittee and empowering me and our colleagues to pursue this very important priority. So, welcome everyone once again to the first hearing. The topic is the path to universal child care. Today, March 2nd marks exactly three years ago that I stood outside the steps with so many of you to rally my intro my universal child care bill, and in those years, we’ve been able to grow, join coalitions, have countless roundtables. We’ve learned so much from one another, and we fought together. Today, with this new subcommittee, the space to emphasize the importance of Early Childhood Education lives right here in the City Council.

Today’s hearing will examine how the administration plans to move towards a universal child care system in New York City. We want to understand how it will define success for its Early Childhood Education programs and ensure investments translate into stable, high-quality child care where everyone from parents to children to providers, are taken care of. And equally as important, this hearing is a space for parents, for providers, for advocates and the public to tell us what’s not working and what would. Going forward, we want this new subcommittee to truly understand every facet of the multiple areas that are related to Early Childhood Education. Child care in New York City is complicated. There’s different agencies involved, different funding streams, different budget cycles, different rules, different workforce structures, and when everything gets lumped together, it’s hard to see what’s really broken. So instead of treating child care like one giant problem, we’re going to take it piece by piece. We want to work together to make this work. We all know that quality child care is important. The Speaker, myself and so many of my colleagues understand that intimately. The first years of a child’s life

literally shapes the foundation for everything that comes next. Investing in high-quality Early Childhood Education isn’t just something that’s nice to have. It leads to better life outcomes that save taxpayer dollars money and is essential to our economy. In January, I stood with the Governor, the Mayor, Speaker Menin while announced plan about setting us on a path to universal child care. Beyond the funding level, however, few details have emerged about how the city would implement the system-wide expansion. So, today, we’ll hear from the Mayor’s Office of Child Care, the Department of Education, advocates, Early Childhood educators, providers, parents, and other interested stakeholders, and we’ll ask what resources are needed to move towards universal child care in New York City, how can we work across agencies to rapidly prepare for system expansion? Good morning to Speaker Menin, Chair Gutiérrez, members of the City Council Committee on Education and Subcommittee on Early Childhood Education, and all Council Members joining today’s hearing. My name is Emmy Liss and I am the Executive Director of the Mayor’s Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education. I’m joined today by Simone Hawkins, Deputy Chancellor for Early Childhood Education at New York City Public Schools. I’m grateful to be here for the subcommittee’s first-ever hearing and for the opportunity to share more about the Mamdani Administration’s vision for universal child care. As we begin today’s hearing, I want to recognize the incredible commitment of Chair Gutiérrez and so many others in the Council who pushed for child care and Early Childhood Education

to be a top priority for city government. Chair Gutiérrez has also been a strong advocate for the Mayor’s Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education, and as I will outline in my testimony today, we believe this office will be critical to mobilizing an all of government approach to implementing universal child care. I also want to recognize the many decades of labor and organizing by child care providers, educators, parents and advocates, many of whom I know will offer testimony later today. We have collectively reached a moment where government is poised to act and implement an expansive vision for universal child care that if successful will be life-changing for parents, educators and our economy and city at large. As a parent to two young children who I’m raising in New York City, I know just how critical universal child care would be. In my testimony today, I plan to outline our vision for universal child care, the role that my office will play in delivering this vision, and how we will work with many partners across city and state government, and the nonprofit and business communities to implement this vision. I will also speak briefly to the legislative proposals being

considered at today’s hearing. I then look forward to your questions and to the testimonies that early care and education providers, advocates, and community members will deliver. Our vision for universal child care is a system in which every family has access to free, high-quality, culturally-responsive care and education for all children under five with care offered in a range of settings and delivered by caregivers and educators who are respected and fairly compensated. Successfully implementing this vision will have a profound impact on our city. Children who have access to high-quality early care and education will build developmentally-appropriate skills that put them on a trajectory for stronger outcomes in elementary school and beyond. Parents will save an average of $26,000 annually which is money they can spend in our local economy and use to build economic security for their families. Universal child care will increase the share of parents in the workforce with more caregivers, and in particular, more mothers likely to seek employment opportunities. Altogether, we expect universal child care to keep young families in our city, reversing the high rates of migration we

see today for families with children under six. And with universal child care, New York City businesses will see lower rates of employee turnover and more stability in their workforce and our overall economic output will grow. This sounds like a fantastical vision, but there’s evidence to support all of our claims. All across the country, including here in New York, there’s demonstrated proof that access to Early Childhood and education boosts children’s social/emotional development, and kindergarten readiness, not to mention their high school graduation rates and long-term employment outcomes. When New York City expanded access to 3K, maternal employment rose in neighborhoods with free preschool education, and mothers were more likely to stay employed even after their child finished Pre-K. Many New York City businesses have seen employee retention rise when their workers have access to child care benefits, driving down their recruitment and training costs. And when Quebec first implemented universal child care over 20 years ago, the increase in income tax revenue exceeded the municipal costs to implement the program, demonstrating the true return on investment for early care and education. In January

of this year, just days after Mayor Mamdani took office, the Governor and Mayor announced a commitment of over $1.2 billion state funding for New York City to put us on the path to universal child care. With these new resources, we will stabilize the child care voucher program. We will ensure every family have access to a high-quality 3K and Pre-K seat this fall with expanded 3K capacity in areas of the city that historically had unmet family demand. We will launch 2K providing high-quality early care and education to approximately 2,000 two-year-olds in Fall 2026. 2K will grow to serve another approximately 10,000 two-year-olds in fall of 2027 for a total of 12,000 children, and by the end of the Mayor’s first term, we will provide access to every two-year-old in the city. We will build this program in partnership with community-based child care providers and home-based family child care providers, and we recognize that as we expand, we also need to address critical operational gaps facing our child care provider community to ensure they have the resources they need. Delivering a responsive and sustainable universal early care and education system will take an all of government approach. This is where the

Mayor’s Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education comes in. My office is responsible for setting the administration’s child care strategy, coordinating work across city agencies to deliver a high-quality early care and education system that is responsive to child care providers and meets family’s needs and collaborating with a range of partners internal and external to city government as well as engaging the public. We will serve as a central hub for citywide policy implementation and coordination across more than a dozen agencies, including New York City Public Schools, the Administration of Children Services, the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, and the Department of Social Services, among many others. Our city agency partners will continue to drive policy and implementation forward and they are experts at what they do. My office will not stand in the way of critical work. We are here to ensure alignment across agencies and to make sure the work is properly resourced and supported. We will also foster strategic partnerships with all levels of government, private entities, nonprofits and foundations, and work closely with families and providers to ensure their voices are represented in

the design and implementation of city policy and programs. Across all of the city’s early care and education work, we will be tracking and monitoring progress to ensure we are on track to meet our goals. As this administration begins our critical work to expand access to high-quality early care and education for all families, we are able to build on a foundation of existing strong programs here in the city. We also recognize there’s opportunity to make this system work far better for families and for child care providers.
